accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE national curriculum in England, English programmes of study Key Stage 3 (pupils should understand how the work of dramatists is communicated effectively through performance and how alternative staging allows for different interpretations of a play) and CCSS ELA RL.6.7 to RL.8.7 (compare a staged or filmed version with the script and evaluate faithfulness and departures). Stage left/right from the actor's view facing the audience, downstage as the front, and the Macbeth 2.1 lines 'Is this a dagger which I see before me' and 'A dagger of the mind, a false creation' were checked against the Folger text.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented drama-study slips: treating the script as the whole play, reading stage left as the audience's left (mirror error), thinking downstage means under the stage, believing only words carry meaning, and judging a production wrong just because it differs. Each appears as a prediction, a refused lab move with a reason, or a tagged challenge option with its own correction.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagstage has its own mechanics: three cue pickers (voice, pause, body) that change a two-figure scene and its mixed-signals feedback, a light dial that relights a scene through warm wash, cold blue and spotlight, a 3x3 stage grid seen from the seats with drag blocking, set-to-aim matching and a production sorter. The 6-token shingle gate passed against every flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner keeps the same two words 'I'm fine.' and sees the meaning flip from hurt to angry as cues change, watches the scene's mood change under each light, finds that stage left lands on their right on the grid, and sorts four real-style stagings of the dagger by what they suggest. The text names what the stage already showed.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: whether the same words can carry two meanings (many expect the words fix the meaning) and which side 'stage left' is from the seats (the mirror error). Each is resolved by the scene itself rather than a told answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers: 'mirror' and 'updown' fix stage geography, 'words' and 'only' teach subtext and delivery, 'warm' and 'nolight' explain lighting effect, 'literal' and 'differ' address faithfulness and interpretation, and 'back' and 'below' correct downstage. Options rotate position each round.

readability.evidence: Learner text reads at FK grade 2.4 and the adult notes at 4.6, both well inside the 6.5 and 9.5 limits, with short sentences while keeping precise terms: subtext, stage directions, blocking, proxemics, upstage, downstage, naturalistic, minimalist, expressionist, interpretation, production.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph does work: the 'I'm fine.' example carries subtext, the stage-geography paragraph gives the actor's-view rule, the Macbeth paragraph models interpretation, the adult notes give curriculum, terms and mistakes. The filler regex gate and the 12% overlap gate both passed.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360px Android width in dark and light themes show the stage, grid, set cards and sorter bins fitting without overlap; all choice buttons are full-size tap targets and the grid accepts tap as well as drag. The walker completed every Show me on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reported no violations in either theme. Every canvas has an aria-label that updates with the scene, the grid and sorter can be driven by buttons without dragging, feedback is written text not colour alone, and the cue buttons and stage figures keep contrast in light and dark.

sources: DfE (2013) National curriculum in England: English programmes of study, Key Stage 3 (Reading: drama and performance)
NGA Center and CCSSO (2010) Common Core State Standards for ELA, RL.6.7, RL.7.7, RL.8.7
Shakespeare, W. Macbeth, Act 2 Scene 1, Folger Shakespeare Library edition
